blocks.text: Line up an SS3 class and measure everyone's height: you get a smooth spread from shortest to tallest with most in the middle. Now ask everyone their blood group: you get four sharp categories and nothing in between. Both are inherited characteristics, but they vary in completely different ways.

blocks.markdown:
## Two patterns of variation

**Continuous variation** gives a smooth range of values with no distinct categories. Height, body mass, skin colour and intelligence are examples. Each is controlled by **many genes acting together** (polygenic inheritance) and is strongly influenced by the **environment** — diet affects height, and nothing about a person's genes fixes their body mass. Plotting the data gives a bell-shaped curve.

**Discontinuous variation** gives a small number of clear-cut categories with no intermediates. ABO blood group, sex, ability to roll the tongue, and the presence of sickle cell haemoglobin are examples. Each is controlled by **one gene, or very few**, and the environment has little or no effect. Plotting the data gives separate bars.

blocks.markdown:
### Sex determination in humans

Of the 23 pairs of human chromosomes, 22 pairs are **autosomes** and one pair is the **sex chromosomes**. A female is **XX** and a male is **XY**.

A female produces only one kind of egg, carrying X. A male produces two kinds of sperm in equal numbers: half carry X and half carry Y. Whichever sperm fertilises the egg determines the sex of the child:

- X sperm + X egg → XX → girl
- Y sperm + X egg → XY → boy

Because the two kinds of sperm are equally numerous, the chance of a boy is 50% at every conception. **The sex of a child is determined by the father**, since only he can supply a Y chromosome — a point worth stating plainly given how often families in Nigeria blame mothers for the sex of their children.

blocks.title: A genetic cross for sex determination
blocks.prompt: Use a Punnett square to show why boys and girls are expected in equal numbers, and state the probability that a couple's fourth child will be a boy if the first three were girls.

steps.text: Write the parental genotypes: mother XX, father XY.
Write the gametes. The mother produces only X eggs. The father produces X and Y sperm in equal numbers.
Combine them. X egg with X sperm gives XX; X egg with Y sperm gives XY. Only two outcomes are possible and they are equally likely.
Read the ratio: 1 XX : 1 XY, that is 1 girl : 1 boy, or a 50% chance of each.

Now the fourth child. Each fertilisation is an independent event: the sperm that wins the race is not influenced by which sperm won three years ago. The probability of a boy is therefore still 1 in 2, or 50%, exactly as for the first child.

blocks.answer: The cross XX × XY gives 1 girl : 1 boy, so each child has a 50% chance of being a boy. Having had three girls does not change the odds for the fourth child, which remain 50%.

blocks.markdown:
### Sex-linked inheritance

The X chromosome is much larger than the Y and carries genes with no counterpart on the Y. Genes for **colour blindness** and **haemophilia** are recessive and lie on the X.

A female has two X chromosomes, so a single faulty allele is masked by the normal one on her other X — she is a **carrier**, unaffected herself. A male has only one X, so if his single copy carries the faulty allele there is no normal allele to mask it and he is affected. This is why colour blindness and haemophilia are far commoner in males, and why an affected boy usually inherits the allele from a carrier mother.

### Sickle cell and multiple alleles

**Sickle cell** inheritance involves the haemoglobin gene, with allele Hb^A for normal haemoglobin and Hb^S for sickle haemoglobin.

- **AA** — normal, healthy.
- **AS** — sickle cell trait (a carrier). Usually healthy, and has some resistance to malaria.
- **SS** — sickle cell anaemia. Red cells distort into a sickle shape when oxygen is low, blocking capillaries and causing severe pain, anaemia and crises.

Two AS parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an SS child at every pregnancy, which is exactly why genotype testing before marriage matters so much in Nigeria.

**ABO blood group** is controlled by **three alleles** of one gene: I^A, I^B and I^O. I^A and I^B are **codominant** with each other — both are expressed in a person who has both, giving group AB — and both are dominant to I^O. So group A is I^A I^A or I^A I^O, group B is I^B I^B or I^B I^O, group AB is I^A I^B, and group O is only I^O I^O.

items: Selective breeding: farmers keep and breed only the highest-yielding cassava, the best egg-laying hens or the cows with the greatest milk yield, so favourable alleles become commoner in the population.
Hybrid vigour: crossing two different pure lines can give offspring stronger and higher-yielding than either parent, as with hybrid maize.
Genetic counselling: couples who both have the AS genotype can be advised of the 1 in 4 risk of an SS child before starting a family.
Blood group testing: matching donor and recipient prevents fatal agglutination during transfusion.
Forensic and paternity testing: DNA profiles and blood groups can exclude a suspected parent, although a blood group match alone cannot prove parentage.

blocks.title: Codominance is not incomplete dominance
blocks.text: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed, so an AB individual has both A and B antigens on the cell surface — not a blend. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is a genuine intermediate, as with the pink four o'clock flower. Examiners often set one against the other.

points: Continuous variation is polygenic, environmentally influenced and gives a smooth range; discontinuous variation is controlled by one or few genes and gives distinct categories.
Females are XX and males XY, so the sex of a child is determined by whether an X-bearing or a Y-bearing sperm fertilises the egg.
Colour blindness and haemophilia are X-linked recessive conditions and are therefore commoner in males.
Sickle cell genotypes are AA (normal), AS (trait, malaria-resistant) and SS (sickle cell anaemia); two AS parents risk an SS child in one pregnancy in four.
ABO blood group involves three alleles, with I^A and I^B codominant and both dominant to I^O.
